questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That I could take the train fairly easy from Copenhagen. A good University with interesting courses. A good food culture and easy to get around and explore different part of the country and neighbouring ones.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It has been way too difficult and time consuming with finding courses that matches and with different ECTS point for each course it is not going to support my further studies when I come home, so that I have sadly used a lot of time on and will still have to take supplementary courses at home.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. For the course description I wished for a more clear one to know the prerequisites as I ended up switching a course that was way to out of my academic scope even though I lived up to all the prerequisites. So I wish, I had that information before hand.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had really good help when I needed to change this course in a late period due to the difficulty of the course. So really happy with all the help I got.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. I had a friend that live in the room during spring and then I just took over that one.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I lived in Brussels, and future exchange students should know that it is very easy to take the train and Brussels is a very nice city. On the other hand it becomes more difficult to social with those living in Leuven as the last train leaves pretty early, so you have to make friends in Brussels as well, but that suited me perfectly as I like to socials more in the weekends than during the week, and in Leuven all social activities are from Sunday-Thursday.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: In the course catalogue for exchange courses you find the ones you like (apply for pre-approval at home university, get all the necessary signatures for the OLA), and then the course is to be found in your ISP, you choose exam dates and they will appear in your Toledo.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I could always reach out to the exchange student advisor, who help really good.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses that I wanted, so that was very nice.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Carefully look at which programs the different courses is under, and then do not take courses from really mathematical programs is you study economics. Choose some courses where the examination is during the semester, as you wont be so stressed during the exam period, and those courses was my favorite ones, as you are active during the semester and really learn actively throughout the period. It also seems like the teacher really get a grasp for what you know and what you do not know, where I find the exams here very strange and old and do not at all resemble the knowledge I need for future work where the internet is a available all the time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was in the harder end of what I am used to, but I really enjoyed the teachers. The student I was very shocked about their lack of engagement when we had group work and sadly I used too much time trying to get in contacts with the student and make group work. I also think it is a culture difference, I was about 5 years older than most of them, and that I could really feel unfortunately.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At my home university UCPH we focus more on applied work and that I really enjoy and find useful, where we never have to learn proofs by heart, but rather the intuition and interpretation of equations. Most people are not going to be a researcher, but rather work in the public or private sector, so I wished the teaching focussed a bit more on that. Why are we not allowed to have notes and scrap paper in the exam? For me it does not make sense with the technology we have in 2025, that we still write with pen and paper with no aids and no visible clock in the exam room to administre the time.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Sustainable development, Industrial Organization, Trading and Exchange, Governance, Data Science for Businesses, Macro-Economics and Economic Policy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sustainable development, best course! Really interactive, I have never learned so much. The course was new thinking in that way the course was structured, the learning method was different, so we both has to write, present, discuss, read etc. why the material really stucked with me. I was so interesting papers and the teachers monitored the discussing very well, but also in a way where you as a student really felt you where heard and listened too.

questions.answer: Non really.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
the public transport. Very cheap when you are a student. To get it is a nightmare as the system is very old, so you need a lot of papers in hand and passport picture size to get it, but ones you have it, it only cost 1 euro to commute to Leuven. Within Brussels it is also possible to get a card valid for all metro, busses and trams for 12 euros unlimited use for a year. 
Only for one of the my classes did I need to purchase a book, so that was cheaper than expected.
Gym was more expensive than expected, but they realy have some nice ones, and they of course are also more expensive. Try Animo!!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I have not tried any of them, so I do not know.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I do not know, because I lived in Brussels and did not engage so much in the social life in Leuven, but I know a lot was arranged.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Everyone talk about a 24-hour run, but again I did not try any, so I do not know.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Brussels if you live in Leuven at check out all the vintage shops, art nouveau houses (all Victor Horta houses are so special - book well in advance especially for Hotel Solvay), experience the jazz and techno music and eat a lot of good food. I would also go to Ghent, Brugge and Antwerpen. Also, take the train to Amsterdam, Paris, Lyon, Marseille - so easy when you are in the middle of western europe.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. In Brussels it is mostly french speaking which I love, and you feel like you are in a french city.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not the most welcoming people, so the attitude can be somewhat rude if you are an outsider, but then again I also met the most welcoming and friendly Belgium people. Figure the trash system can be difficult and you would think that the city of EU would have developed a more clever system, where it was not out in the open, but in the ground or in big trash bins. They do not collect their dog poop, and many have a dog, so be careful where you step.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love the jazz and techno mix, and bying a croissant in Brussels by French speaking people and then jump on the train to Leuven, where people speak Dutch and the architecture in this little city is so special and beautiful.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Only go if you are ready to use a lot of time on figuring out courses and ready to fail a few. There system is completely different from ours, so half of their grades are failing grades and you are being graded in a way where are not taught at in UCPH. I think I used too much time on school it self, and figuring out the school system, so I barely had time to also enjoy myself in the way I experienced, which I really regret. I think at other places you could go there will be a better balance between school and enjoying yourself. At least I am never this worried about exams and passing at my home university - I know if I study and follow the course, the chance that I would fail is very little, where here I am so scared to fail half of my courses, even though I really have studied throughout the semester and prepared weeks in advance for the exam.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you do not like to party during the day and study in the weekend, really think about living in Brussel instead.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: If I pass all my exams that would be the most rewarding part.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out the school system and to make it match with mine a home since courses here are rewarded 6 and 3 ECTS and at home it is 7,5 ECTS.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
